originalTitle: The Fairphone 6 Plus is the midrange phone we desperately needed

content: The Fairphone 6 Plus feels like an extremely average midrange Android phone and I couldn’t be more thrilled. The mission has always been admirable. Fairphone seeks out ethically sourced materials and offers a high degree of repairability for its devices. But the phones themselves required a lot of sacrifices, like putting up with underpowered processors and bad cameras, in order to embrace the sustainability mission. The latest generations of Fairphone have inched toward closing that gap, and the 6 Plus achieves two huge milestones: It feels very much like using a middling Android phone, and it’s actually on sale in the US. The 6 Plus is a light update to last year’s Fairphone 6, which my colleague Dominic Preston reviewed and found very easy to recommend. The 6 Plus builds on it with a newer midrange Snapdragon chipset and a new color treatment. Fairphone says it’s cobalt; we know it around these parts as blurple. Otherwise, the phone is basically the same, and the replacement parts sold by Fairphone work interchangeably with both models. But above all, this phone is just fine. It runs about as fast as your typical mid-tier Razr or A-series Pixel. It offers a pleasantly close-to-stock version of Android free of bloat or gimmicky AI features. It’s just a phone. And that’s great. [Product: Fairphone 6 Plus | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H9M1V2BK?tag=theverge02-20, https://us.fairphone.com/the-fairphone-gen-6-plus] I know, calling this a midrange phone when it’s priced at $649 might feel like a stretch. At best, it’s at the very top of the midrange class. But RAMageddon has done a real number on phone prices over the past year, and it’s not over yet. Given that the phone comes with 12GB of RAM, a five-year warranty, and up to six OS upgrades, that price feels more manageable.  Also, you don’t need to add AppleCare or whatever to that price. You are the AppleCare. The 6 Plus has 12 user-replaceable parts including the battery, screen, USB-C port, and all three cameras. The repairs are extremely beginner-friendly — if you can use the tiny included screwdriver and follow some easy-to-parse directions, you won’t have a problem. The price of these parts compared to the cost of repairing a Google Pixel or Samsung Galaxy phone range from a pretty good deal to a hell of a good deal. Without an extended warranty of some kind, a battery replacement would typically cost in the ballpark of $100 to $180; Fairphone charges $39.99 for a new battery. A screen repair ranges from $100 to nearly $300; a new display from Fairphone costs $89.99. Add in the entirely reasonable cost of 30 minutes of your own labor (if that), and the long-term value of this phone starts looking pretty good. $649 is also a bargain compared to the $899 that the Fairphone 6 costs in the US. It was only offered preloaded with the privacy-minded /e/OS, which is a de-Googled version of Android made by a company called Murena. It’s not really for the faint of heart, and that price was pretty hard to swallow. But Fairphone is selling the 6 Plus directly in the US, with full support for T-Mobile and AT&T. I’ve had no trouble using it with my Verizon SIM for the past week, though it’s not certified on the network. [Image: More than meets the eye. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268725_Fairphone_6_Plus_review_AJohnson_0004.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Knowing how easy it is to replace parts of this phone as it ages actually required me to think a bit differently while I was using it. Battery life is just okay. I usually got through most days of light-to-moderate use with 60 percent left at bedtime. I did turn on every battery-draining feature I could think of, including the always-on display, higher screen refresh rate, and light mode. Those are all off by default, and probably for good reason. Normally I’d be pretty concerned about what that battery performance would look like in a few years.  But there’s an easy fix: Just swap the battery yourself. No trip to the repair shop, no time away from your phone. Most phones would benefit from a new battery after a few years of continuous use anyway; at least with this one you can do it yourself and pay a lot less. The 6 Plus comes with way fewer compromises than early versions of the Fairphone did. The first iterations came with outdated designs, poor-quality cameras, and previous-gen displays. Things have steadily improved, but there are still some tradeoffs hanging around. The phone is rated IP55, which equates to mostly dust-resistant and mostly water-resistant, but not fully protected. Sealing up the phone completely and still offering easy repairability would be difficult, maybe impossible. That’s bad news, item one. Item two: no wireless charging, and likewise no ring of magnets a la Qi2 or MagSafe. I’m growing partial to an easily removable PopSocket on my phone, so I missed having that option here. Moving along: The screen is thoroughly decent, though it doesn’t get quite as bright in daylight as some of the nicest ones out there. The speakers are tinny. And even after more than a week with this phone, I still haven’t learned the muscle memory of finding the wake button / fingerprint scanner without looking, since it sits basically flush with the side of the phone.  [Image: The wake button is a little hard to find by memory. But 10/10 for this physical slider. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268725_Fairphone_6_Plus_review_AJohnson_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Snapdragon 7S Gen 4 chipset handled the basic demands of modern life. If you poke around the edges you can find where this chipset falls short of the very best SoCs — which you can come by in devices that don’t cost much more than the Fairphone 6 Plus. Google Maps runs a little stuttery on my car’s infotainment screen when I run it with wired Android Auto, and there’s a bit of juddering as I scroll around my town in Pocket City 2. chineseTitle: Fairphone 6 Plus 是我们迫切需要的中端手机
chineseSummary: Fairphone 6 Plus 感觉就像一款极其普通的中端 Android 手机，我对此感到非常兴奋。使命始终令人钦佩。 Fairphone 寻求符合道德标准的材料，并为其设备提供高度的可修复性。但手机本身需要做出很多牺牲，比如忍受动力不足的处理器 […]
chineseContent: Fairphone 6 Plus 感觉就像一款极其普通的中端 Android 手机，我对此感到非常兴奋。使命始终令人钦佩。 Fairphone 寻求符合道德标准的材料，并为其设备提供高度的可修复性。但手机本身需要做出很多牺牲，比如忍受动力不足的处理器和糟糕的相机，才能完成可持续发展的使命。最新一代的 Fairphone 已经逐渐缩小了这一差距，而 6 Plus 实现了两个巨大的里程碑：它的感觉非常像使用中等水平的 Android 手机，而且它实际上在美国有售。 6 Plus 是去年 Fairphone 6 的轻微更新，我的同事多米尼克·普雷斯顿 (Dominic Preston) 对其进行了评测，发现非常容易推荐。 6 Plus 在此基础上配备了更新的中端 Snapdragon 芯片组和新的色彩处理。 Fairphone 说它是钴；我们知道这些部分周围是模糊的。除此之外，这款手机基本上是相同的，Fairphone 出售的替换零件可以与这两种型号互换使用。但最重要的是，这款手机还不错。它的运行速度与典型的中端 Razr 或 A 系列 Pixel 一样快。它提供了一个令人愉悦的接近原生版本的 Android，没有臃肿或花哨的人工智能功能。这只是一部电话。那太好了。 [产品：Fairphone 6 Plus | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H9M1V2BK?tag=theverge02-20，https://us.fairphone.com/the-fairphone-gen-6-plus]我知道，当它的售价为 649 美元时，将其称为中端手机可能会让人感觉有些牵强。充其量，它处于中端类别的最顶端。但 RAMgeddon 对过去一年的手机价格做了真实的统计，而且还没有结束。考虑到这款手机配备 12GB RAM、五年保修和最多六次操作系统升级，这个价格感觉更容易管理
